title: Industrial IoT: From Sensor Data to Better Operational Decisions
excerpt: An industrial IoT project should start with an operational question. Learn how to connect the right assets, establish reliable data, and turn monitoring into a practical response workflow.
seoTitle: Industrial IoT: From Sensor Data to Decisions | Najhum
seoDescription: Plan an industrial IoT pilot around asset priorities, reliable sensor data, cybersecurity, and clear response workflows with this practical guide.
coverAlt: Engineer inspecting a wireless sensor on pipework at an industrial processing site.
content:
A connected factory can produce thousands of readings while leaving its operators with the same unanswered questions. Which asset needs attention? Is the process behaving normally? Who should investigate an exception?

A useful industrial IoT programme starts by choosing a decision to improve. Sensors, connectivity, and dashboards then become parts of a defined operating process. The following approach is a planning framework for that work, rather than a promise that collecting more data will automatically improve performance.

Start with one operational question

Choose a situation the team already recognises: an unexpected motor stoppage, an uncertain tank level, or a temperature excursion that takes too long to investigate. Describe what happens today, who responds, and which information is missing when the issue occurs.

Write a short objective such as: “When the storage level changes outside its expected operating pattern, the shift supervisor should receive enough context to decide whether an inspection is needed.” This is more useful than a general goal to make the plant smart.

Connect the signal to the asset

For the pilot, create an asset register that links each reading to a specific machine, location, unit of measurement, and responsible team. Record where the sensor is installed and what its reading actually represents. A surface temperature, for example, should not be labelled as a direct measurement of internal process temperature.

Ask the installation team to document normal operating conditions and any limitations discovered during commissioning. This gives operators a way to distinguish a genuine process change from a change in measurement conditions.

Make data quality visible

A dashboard should help people recognise missing, stale, or implausible readings. Decide how the pilot will show the last successful update and how it will distinguish equipment that is offline from equipment that is operating normally.

  • Use consistent timestamps and engineering units.
  • Record changes to sensor placement and configuration.
  • Compare selected readings with an appropriate reference during commissioning.
  • Define who investigates communication gaps and unreliable measurements.

Plan cybersecurity before expanding

NIST’s IoT device baseline identifies capabilities including device identification, configuration, data protection, access control, software updates, and cybersecurity-state awareness. Use these as prompts when evaluating devices and supplier support. The baseline is a starting point for requirements, not proof that a particular deployment is secure.

For the pilot, document who can access device settings, how credentials are managed, and who owns software maintenance. Agree on these responsibilities before adding more sites or assets.

Turn an alert into an assigned action

Every important alert needs an owner, a first investigation step, and a closure record. Include the affected asset, the relevant trend, and the operating context. During the pilot, review alerts with the people who receive them and remove notifications that do not lead to a useful decision.

Evaluate the project using measures the team can check: time taken to investigate an event, completeness of the asset records, or the proportion of alerts that resulted in a documented response. Expand when the workflow is useful and repeatable.

title: Smart Building Monitoring: Start with the Systems People Depend On
excerpt: A practical guide to prioritising HVAC, water, comfort, and equipment monitoring, with clear responsibilities and an operating workflow that facilities teams can use.
seoTitle: Smart Building Monitoring: A Practical Guide | Najhum
seoDescription: Build a practical smart building monitoring plan for HVAC, water, and comfort. Prioritise important systems and connect alerts to facilities workflows.
coverAlt: Facilities engineer reviewing equipment in a building mechanical room.
content:
Buildings are experienced through everyday details: a comfortable meeting room, reliable water supply, working ventilation, and equipment that receives attention before an issue becomes disruptive. A monitoring project is most useful when it connects those experiences to the systems the facilities team manages.

Begin by mapping the services people depend on. The aim is to give the team a clearer investigation path when something changes, while keeping the project manageable enough to commission and maintain properly.

Prioritise services before selecting devices

List the building’s main operational concerns and rank them with the facilities team. A hotel may prioritise guest-room comfort and refrigeration. An office may focus on air-handling schedules and water systems. A storage facility may care most about conditions in particular zones.

For each concern, identify the equipment involved, the current inspection process, and the person who owns the response. This helps determine whether the next step is additional sensing, access to existing building-management data, or a change to the maintenance workflow.

Use HVAC monitoring to support investigation

The U.S. Department of Energy describes HVAC commissioning as checking whether building systems operate in accordance with their design and engineering requirements. Monitoring should support that verification, with readings that can be interpreted against the intended operating sequence.

For example, if an air-handling unit runs after its expected schedule, the investigation should consider occupancy requirements, override settings, and the control sequence. A running signal alone does not establish that the equipment is wasting energy or operating incorrectly.

Give water events enough context

Water monitoring can involve different questions: Is a tank level changing as expected? Is a pump available? Is a suspected leak indication linked to a particular area? Define which question each measurement answers and how the team will verify an exception.

Develop a simple response plan for each monitored system. Identify the contact person, the inspection location, and the escalation route. Where automatic control is proposed, have the relevant specialists review the control logic and its failure behaviour before it is enabled.

Avoid a dashboard full of unexplained numbers

Organise the interface around the building’s layout and services. Asset names should match the labels used by maintenance staff. Show units, recent trends, and the age of the latest reading so the team can understand whether the information is suitable for a decision.

  • Use a consistent naming convention for floors, zones, and equipment.
  • Document which sensors represent a room and which represent equipment.
  • Review thresholds with the team responsible for responding.
  • Keep a record of investigations and the actions taken.

Review the operating process after the pilot

Start with one service or building zone and review the results with facilities staff. Ask whether alerts were understandable, whether the right person received them, and whether the information reduced uncertainty during an inspection.

A successful pilot should leave behind more than a dashboard: an asset map, a maintained set of measurements, and a response process that the next shift can follow.

title: Energy Monitoring: Build a Baseline Before You Make Changes
excerpt: Understand the difference between energy use and demand, choose useful metering boundaries, and create a practical review process before claiming efficiency improvements.
seoDescription: Learn how to plan energy monitoring, choose useful submetering boundaries, establish a baseline, and assess changes without making unsupported savings claims.
coverAlt: Engineer reviewing energy metering on closed electrical switchgear.
content:
An electricity bill tells you what a site consumed over a billing period. It may not explain which operating patterns contributed to that result. Energy monitoring is a way to ask more precise questions, provided the readings are connected to useful boundaries and reviewed by people who can act on them.

Before choosing a dashboard or announcing a reduction target, define what you want to understand. You might want to investigate after-hours operation, compare similar production periods, or separate a major equipment group from the rest of the site.

Choose the boundary of the question

Building-level, distribution-level, and end-use metering answer different questions. The U.S. Department of Energy’s metering guidance discusses these levels and the importance of a planned metering programme. A site-wide reading gives an overall picture; a more specific measurement can support investigation of an individual area or system.

Start with a diagram of the electrical distribution and label the boundaries you can measure reliably. Decide which questions can be answered with existing data before specifying additional meters. Have electrical work assessed and carried out by the appropriate qualified professionals.

Keep energy and demand separate

Energy use, commonly expressed in kilowatt-hours, describes electricity consumed over time. Power, commonly expressed in kilowatts, describes the rate of use. Billing demand can depend on the utility’s measurement interval and tariff rules, so confirm those details before interpreting a peak on a dashboard as a billing event.

Use clear labels and retain the measurement interval with the data. A monthly total and a short-interval reading should not appear as interchangeable indicators.

Build a baseline with operating context

Select an initial review period and record the conditions that matter to the site. These might include opening hours, occupied area, production activity, or unusual shutdowns. Keep notes on changes that would affect a comparison.

For example, a lower weekly energy total may reflect fewer operating hours rather than an efficiency improvement. A useful review asks what changed in the operation as well as what changed in the meter reading. Where a formal savings claim is required, agree on a suitable measurement and verification method with the responsible specialists.

Investigate one pattern at a time

Choose an observation that the team can investigate without disrupting the site. Look at whether an equipment group follows its intended schedule or whether an unexpected overnight load has an identifiable cause. Treat the pattern as an investigation prompt, not as a diagnosis.

  • Confirm that timestamps and meter labels are correct.
  • Check for missing intervals and changes in data collection.
  • Record the proposed operational change and who approved it.
  • Compare the result over a suitable period with relevant operating conditions noted.

Make the review a recurring responsibility

A meter does not produce a better operating outcome by itself. Give a named team responsibility for reviewing trends, recording actions, and checking whether the monitoring system remains reliable.

Use the first monitoring phase to build a repeatable review process. Expand the metering plan when additional measurements will answer a defined question, rather than simply adding more charts.

title: Planning EV Charging: Think Beyond the Charger
excerpt: A charging project needs an operating model as well as hardware. Plan for driver needs, electrical capacity, charger compatibility, and the team that will support the network.
seoTitle: Planning EV Charging Infrastructure & Operations | Najhum
seoDescription: Plan an EV charging project around driver needs, electrical capacity, OCPP compatibility, site operations, and maintenance before selecting hardware.
coverAlt: Electric vehicles connected to chargers beneath a commercial parking canopy.
content:
A charger is one visible part of an EV charging service. The experience also depends on where drivers park, how long they stay, whether charging can start successfully, and who resolves an issue when it cannot.

Planning should therefore begin with the people and operating conditions at the site. The goal is to choose an appropriate system and support process, rather than treating the number of installed chargers as the only measure of readiness.

Define who will charge and when

A workplace, hotel, residential development, and fleet depot can have very different priorities. Describe the expected users, the time they usually spend on site, and how charging spaces will be managed. Include accessibility, signage, and access arrangements in the site discussion.

For a fleet, identify departure requirements and operational constraints. For guest charging, consider how a driver will find the charger, understand the service, and ask for help. These questions should inform the requirements given to hardware and software suppliers.

Assess the electrical site before choosing scale

Have qualified electrical specialists assess the available capacity, distribution arrangements, proposed installation locations, and applicable approval requirements. Ask them to identify which assumptions need verification before the design is finalised.

Where load management is proposed, document what will be measured, how limits will be enforced, and how the system should behave if communication is interrupted. Do not assume that software removes the need for a suitable electrical design or local approvals.

Check compatibility as a complete system

The Open Charge Alliance maintains OCPP, a protocol used for communication between charging stations and charging-management systems. Protocol versions and supported functions differ. Specifying OCPP is a useful starting point, but a version label alone does not prove that every required function will work across a chosen combination of equipment and software.

Prepare acceptance tests around your intended operation. Ask suppliers to demonstrate the required start and stop flows, session records, fault reporting, and any selected smart-charging functions using the proposed configuration.

Make day-to-day ownership explicit

Write down who is responsible for the charging service. This may involve the site owner, facilities team, software operator, installation contractor, and maintenance provider. Avoid leaving a gap between the person who receives a fault notification and the person authorised to resolve it.

  • Define how drivers report a problem and receive assistance.
  • Assign responsibility for checking faults and connectivity.
  • Agree on access for inspection and maintenance.
  • Decide how service information and operational records will be reviewed.

Commission the driver journey

Test the experience from arrival through the end of a session. Check signs, instructions, access steps, charging initiation, and the information shown to the driver. Include a controlled failure scenario so the support process is tested alongside the normal experience.

Review a pilot period before expanding. Use the observations to refine the design, the management workflow, and the responsibilities of each service provider.

title: Precision Irrigation: Put Soil Data in Context
excerpt: Soil-moisture readings become more useful when they are connected to crop needs, field conditions, and irrigation records. Build a monitoring approach that supports agronomic judgement.
seoTitle: Precision Irrigation & Soil Moisture Monitoring | Najhum
seoDescription: Plan precision irrigation using soil-moisture trends, representative sensor placement, irrigation records, and field checks that support informed decisions.
coverAlt: Soil moisture monitoring device and drip irrigation lines among healthy crops.
content:
A soil-moisture reading is a measurement from a particular place at a particular time. To support an irrigation decision, it needs context: the crop, the root zone, the soil, recent irrigation, and what is happening elsewhere in the field.

A precision-irrigation project should make that context easier to review. Begin with a monitoring plan that supports the farm team’s judgement, then consider automation only after the measurements and operating process have been checked.

Start with the management zones

Discuss the field with the people who know it. Identify differences in soil, terrain, crop development, and irrigation layout. Record where the team already observes uneven drying or inconsistent water delivery.

Use that discussion to define the zones you want to understand. One convenient sensor location should not automatically be treated as representative of an entire farm. Ask an agronomist or irrigation specialist to help determine suitable locations and measurement depths for the crop and soil.

Treat installation as part of measurement quality

University of Minnesota Extension’s soil-moisture guidance emphasises sensor placement and installation, including good contact with the surrounding soil. It also recommends interpreting measurements alongside irrigation-scheduling information. These principles are useful prompts for planning; crop thresholds and local decisions still need to fit the farm’s conditions.

Keep an installation record for every sensor. Include its location, depth, model, configuration, and the zone it is intended to represent. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions and review the readings with field observations before relying on them.

Review trends alongside irrigation events

A single number may not explain whether an irrigation event had the intended effect. Review how readings change before and after watering and compare those observations with the irrigation record.

Where flow or pressure is measured, use those readings to support investigation of water delivery. A valve command is an instruction; it does not, by itself, establish how much water reached the crop. Define which measurements are needed to check the outcome at your site.

Make remote control a separate decision

Remote visibility and automatic irrigation are different project stages. Before enabling control, agree on permissions, manual override arrangements, and the response to missing or unreliable sensor readings.

Have the irrigation and agronomy specialists review any proposed control rules. Document how pump and valve operation will be checked and who can stop the system when field conditions differ from the assumptions in the schedule.

  • Maintain a clear map of sensors, valves, and irrigation zones.
  • Keep records of irrigation events and field observations.
  • Investigate unexpected readings before changing thresholds.
  • Review the monitoring plan as crops and seasonal conditions change.

Evaluate a season, not just a dashboard

Choose a manageable pilot zone and decide what information the team will record. Review the usefulness of the data, the reliability of communication, and whether the monitoring process improved the clarity of irrigation decisions.

Avoid promising a universal water-saving percentage. Outcomes depend on the starting conditions, crop, equipment, and management changes. A measured trial gives the farm a stronger basis for deciding what to expand.
